case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s second-or-successive gatekeeping provisions bar federal prisoners from raising in a later §2255 motion a claim that was already presented in a prior application for authorization, and whether the Supreme Court can review a court of appeals’ authorization decision despite §2244(b)(3)(E).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1) and §2244(b)(3)(E), as incorporated (or not) into federal-prisoner postconviction practice through 28 U.S.C. §2255(h) (and the related timing rule in §2255(f)(3) discussed by the government).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1)—which by its text applies to state-prisoner habeas petitions under §2254—does not apply to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive §2255 motions; instead, federal prisoners are governed by §2255(h)’s two express authorization categories, and importing §2244(b)(1) would add an extra, judge-made hurdle Congress did not include and would create conflict/superfluity with §2255(h). He further contends the Court can and should reach the merits because the Eleventh Circuit’s disposition was not a merits ‘denial’ triggering §2244(b)(3)(E), and/or because §2244(b)(3)(E) should not be read to strip certiorari jurisdiction absent a clear statement (given Article III/Exceptions Clause concerns and the need for uniformity in federal law).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar applies in the §2255 second-or-successive context, so if a federal prisoner previously presented the same claim in an earlier authorization application, it must be dismissed when re-presented. The government emphasizes AEDPA’s finality-focused design, contending it is neither unfair nor unusual that even diligent prisoners may fail to benefit from later legal developments (citing AEDPA’s one-year clock in §2255(f)(3) and Dodd’s ‘harsh result’ rationale). On jurisdiction, the respondent maintains §2244(b)(3)(E) precludes Supreme Court certiorari review of courts of appeals’ grant/denial of authorization to file successive §2255 motions.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (statement respecting denial of certiorari)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (statement respecting denial of original habeas)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest textual point against me: §2244(b)(1) expressly speaks only to §2254, and §2255(h) enumerates just two substantive predicates. But I do not read §2255(h)’s requirement that a successive motion proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244” as importing merely a ministerial filing procedure; in AEDPA’s integrated gatekeeping design, that cross-reference is best understood to carry the baseline anti-relitigation principle that gives the certification decision operative effect, as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize. On jurisdiction, Justice Barrett’s attempt to characterize antecedent-coverage errors as outside a “grant or denial” runs headlong into §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical “shall not” language, and Felker counsels minimalism here: enforce Congress’s clear withdrawal of certiorari rather than crafting implied carveouts that risk rewriting the scheme. Under my institutional-legitimacy approach, the narrower course is to apply the statute as written in its structural context and leave any perceived gap or harshness to Congress.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: §2244(b)(1) expressly governs only successive applications “under section 2254,” and §2255(h) enumerates two predicates. But §2255(h) also commands that a successive motion may proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244,” and in an integrated statutory scheme that cross-reference most naturally incorporates the gatekeeping regime’s core anti-relitigation function; otherwise Congress created a certification process that invites endless resubmission of the same claim, an implausible reading for AEDPA’s finality framework. Justice Barrett’s proposed “antecedent legal error” carveout from §2244(b)(3)(E) cannot be squared with the provision’s categorical bar on certiorari from a “grant or denial,” and Felker treated that withdrawal as effective without implying an exception for threshold mistakes. Dodd and Jones reinforce that AEDPA’s harshness is a legislative choice and that we are not free, under the guise of avoidance or workability, to add judicial review mechanisms Congress withdrew or to narrow clear jurisdiction-stripping text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest textual point: §2244(b)(1) speaks expressly to §2254, and §2255(h) enumerates only two substantive predicates. But that objection does not defeat the more natural integrated reading Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas articulate—§2255(h)’s command that a successive motion proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244” incorporates the essential anti-relitigation feature that makes the certification gatekeeping real rather than an endlessly renewable request process that defeats AEDPA’s finality design. On jurisdiction, Justice Barrett’s effort to recharacterize antecedent legal-error determinations as something other than a “grant or denial” cannot be squared with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical “shall not” language, and Felker supports enforcing that withdrawal of certiorari review as written rather than creating an implied carveout. Workability tools like “abuse of the writ” or law-of-the-case (as Justice Kagan suggests) are not a substitute for the statute’s own integrated certification regime when Congress has chosen strict gatekeeping and finality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the integrated-scheme/finality concern: without an anti-repetition rule, prisoners might recycle identical authorization requests. But that practical worry cannot justify importing §2244(b)(1)’s expressly §2254-limited relitigation bar into §2255(h), which enumerates only two substantive predicates and incorporates “certified as provided” only as a procedural mechanism—exactly as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize—so the Respondents’ reading adds a third, atextual barrier and creates surplusage. On jurisdiction, Justice Thomas’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical “shall not” and Felker is serious, yet Felker cuts for enforcing clear limits as written, not extending certiorari-stripping to antecedent coverage mistakes absent a clear statement; insulating threshold legal errors in a pro se gatekeeping context has too high a real-world cost for access to justice. Dodd and Jones underscore AEDPA’s harshness, but they counsel textual fidelity, not expanding harshness by implication when Congress chose not to extend §2244(b)(1) to §2255.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the integrated-scheme/workability concern: absent some constraint, prisoners could serially re-present identical authorization requests. But under a pragmatic textualism, that concern cannot justify treating §2255(h)’s procedural instruction—“certified as provided in section 2244”—as silently importing §2244(b)(1)’s §2254-only substantive relitigation bar, because Congress expressly limited (b)(1) to §2254 and separately enumerated only two predicates in §2255(h). Felker, invoked by the Chief and Justice Thomas, reinforces that we must enforce clear jurisdiction-stripping when Congress plainly does so; it does not support expanding a limited cross-reference into additional substantive and jurisdictional limits that Congress did not clearly extend to §2255. The administrability problem can be handled through ordinary anti-abuse tools (e.g., rejecting repetitive, unchanged requests) without rewriting AEDPA’s carefully differentiated §2254/§2255 scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is structural: reading §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” to import an anti-relitigation baseline would better serve AEDPA’s finality objectives and avoid serial, identical authorization requests. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the enacted text matters: §2244(b)(1) is expressly limited to §2254 applications, and treating §2255(h)’s procedural cross-reference as silently adding a third substantive bar (beyond §2255(h)(1)–(2)) is atextual and creates surplusage by effectively rewriting Congress’s enumerated predicates. Felker, invoked by Justice Alito and the Chief Justice, reinforces that we enforce clear jurisdiction-stripping when Congress speaks clearly; it does not justify expanding §2244(b)(3)(E) or (b)(1) beyond their terms via implication from a limited cross-reference. Workability concerns about repetitive filings can be addressed through ordinary judicial administration, but they cannot supply missing statutory text under a textualist/originalist approach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the best textual point: §2244(b)(1) expressly speaks only to successive “application[s] under section 2254,” and §2255(h) lists just two predicates. But that does not defeat the Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s structural and administrability concern that, absent an anti-repetition constraint, identical claims can be endlessly repackaged through renewed authorization requests, undermining AEDPA’s finality-centered gatekeeping; §2255(h)’s requirement that a successive motion proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244” is most naturally read to incorporate the baseline one-claim/one-certification feature of the §2244 gatekeeping regime. On jurisdiction, Justice Barrett’s “antecedent legal error” carveout is hard to square with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar on certiorari from a “grant or denial” of authorization, and Felker supports enforcing Congress’s explicit withdrawal rather than implying an exception that would effectively rewrite (E). Given my institutionalist approach, the text-structure fit and the need for a workable, finality-protecting gatekeeping system keep me with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s integrated-scheme/finality concern about serial, repetitive authorization requests is the strongest point for Respondent, but under a textualist approach it cannot justify treating §2255(h)’s cross-reference to certification “as provided in section 2244” as silently importing §2244(b)(1)’s §2254-only relitigation bar and thereby adding a third substantive hurdle beyond §2255(h)(1)–(2). Justice Thomas’s reliance on Dodd and Jones v. Hendrix cuts the same way for me: AEDPA may be stringent, but those cases reinforce fidelity to the enacted text rather than augmenting it by implication to make the scheme more workable. On jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by Roberts/Thomas that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical language forecloses review of an antecedent coverage mistake (whether (b)(1) applies at all); Felker supports enforcing Congress’s certiorari bar as to true grants/denials while not extending it, absent clearer words, to insulate threshold legal errors about the regime’s scope. Workability can be addressed through ordinary nonstatutory doctrines (e.g., law-of-the-case/abuse of process), but we should not rewrite AEDPA’s carefully cabined §2254/§2255 distinctions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s integrated-scheme/finality concern seriously—serial, identical authorization requests would be an administrability problem—but that policy pressure cannot overcome the atextual move they propose: §2244(b)(1) is expressly limited to §2254, and reading §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” to import that substantive relitigation bar would add a third hurdle beyond §2255(h)(1)–(2) and create surplusage. On jurisdiction, Justice Thomas’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical language and Felker is the strongest point for Respondent, yet I remain persuaded by Justice Barrett’s distinction between unreviewable merits-like “grant or denial” determinations and reviewable antecedent, coverage errors about what gatekeeping rules apply in the first place—especially given the fairness stakes of unreviewable, often pro se, screening decisions. Dodd and Jones, as Thomas emphasizes, underscore AEDPA’s rigor, but they cut for me in favor of enforcing the rigor Congress actually wrote, not expanding it by implication in a way that risks insulating threshold legal mistakes from any corrective review.

John Roberts.reasoning: On Question 2, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides that the grant or denial of authorization by a court of appeals “shall not be the subject of … a petition for a writ of certiorari,” and under Felker v. Turpin we have construed AEDPA’s jurisdiction-stripping provisions as effective with respect to certiorari review while preserving only this Court’s original-habeas authority. Exercising restraint and protecting institutional legitimacy, I would not adopt an Exceptions Clause-limiting construction where the statute’s text is clear and Felker already supplies the relevant framework. On Question 1, AEDPA’s finality-driven structure supports applying a relitigation bar in the second-or-successive §2255 context, and reading §2255(h) to incorporate the gatekeeping regime—including §2244(b)(1)’s bar on re-presenting previously presented claims—avoids turning the authorization process into an advisory exercise and aligns with AEDPA’s strict timing rules recognized in Dodd v. United States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of AEDPA indicate that Congress intended the courts of appeals’ gatekeeping decisions on second-or-successive collateral attacks to be final and unreviewable by certiorari: §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides such decisions “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari,” and nothing in §2255(h) supplies an alternative route for Supreme Court review. Consistent with Felker v. Turpin, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s jurisdiction-stripping is valid as written, especially where original habeas remains as the narrow constitutional backstop discussed in Felker, and this Court should not create a clear-statement escape hatch contrary to the enacted text. On the merits of the gatekeeping rules, reading AEDPA to prevent repetitive presentation of the same claim accords with the statute’s design to restrict successive litigation; importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar into the §2255(h) context best fits AEDPA’s finality-focused framework and avoids making the authorization process a vehicle for serial re-presentation of identical claims. This Court’s adherence to AEDPA’s strict limits, even when they yield harsh results, is reflected in Dodd v. United States and reinforced by Jones v. Hendrix’s insistence that prisoners must live with the collateral-review boundaries Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Textually and structurally, AEDPA’s design is to sharply limit repetitive collateral attacks, and §2255(h)’s incorporation of the §2244(b)(3) authorization mechanism is best read to bring with it the relitigation bar of §2244(b)(1) for claims previously “presented,” otherwise prisoners could recycle the same claim through repeated authorization applications and defeat finality. The government’s position fits AEDPA’s practical consequences and finality focus recognized in Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353 (2005), even if the result is harsh for prisoners who later benefit from legal developments. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides that gatekeeping decisions “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari,” and Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996), upheld Congress’s power to restrict certiorari review in this context while leaving any residual review to extraordinary avenues such as original habeas. Reading (E) as a clear withdrawal of certiorari jurisdiction avoids rewriting the statute and preserves AEDPA’s gatekeeping scheme as Congress enacted it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs state-prisoner "application[s]" under §2254, and Congress chose in §2255(h) to specify only two narrow authorization categories for federal prisoners; importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar into §2255 would add an extra hurdle Congress did not enact and risk superfluity with §2255(h)’s carefully drawn scheme. On Supreme Court review, I would construe §2244(b)(3)(E) narrowly to avoid insulating legally erroneous gatekeeping rulings from any corrective review—especially where the court of appeals denies authorization based on a mistaken threshold view of what gatekeeping rules apply—consistent with Felker’s approach of reading AEDPA to avert serious Article III/Exceptions Clause concerns while preserving the Court’s essential role in ensuring uniform federal law. AEDPA’s finality interests cannot justify a regime in which vulnerable or unrepresented prisoners lose any meaningful chance to benefit from intervening decisions because of procedural relitigation rules that Congress did not clearly extend to §2255. Accordingly, I would reverse and allow Bowe’s claim to proceed under §2255(h) (and review the authorization decision notwithstanding §2244(b)(3)(E) as properly construed).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: On Question 1, §2244(b)(1) by its terms governs "a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254," and §2255(h) incorporates only the provisions of §2244 that "provide[]" for certification by a court of appeals; importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar into §2255 adds a third substantive hurdle beyond §2255(h)(1)-(2) and creates avoidable superfluity and mismatch with Congress’s carefully enumerated authorization categories. On Question 2, Felker shows Congress can restrict routes of review, but it also emphasizes reading AEDPA not to foreclose all Supreme Court supervisory capacity absent a clear statement; §2255(h) contains no express “appeal or certiorari” bar and therefore does not clearly carry §2244(b)(3)(E) over into the §2255 context. Interpreting §2255(h) to silently incorporate §2244(b)(3)(E) would raise unnecessary Exceptions Clause and uniformity concerns, especially after Jones v. Hendrix narrowed alternative avenues, and the narrower textual reading avoids those constitutional and workability problems. The more coherent, workable compromise is to hold §2244(b)(1) inapplicable to §2255 motions and permit this Court’s review because §2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar is not incorporated by §2255(h).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) says it applies to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) instead sets out two—and only two—authorization predicates for federal prisoners; reading §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar into §2255 would add atextual, extra gatekeeping rule Congress did not enact and risk surplusage against §2255(h)’s carefully drawn limits. While AEDPA is designed to promote finality, this Court’s job is to enforce the statute’s enacted text, not to broaden it by implication—especially in a postconviction regime where clear rules and the rule-of-lenity impulse counsel against expanding bars on review. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) should be read narrowly to preclude certiorari review only of true grant/denial “decision[s]…under this paragraph,” and Felker v. Turpin supports construing AEDPA’s review-limiting provisions to avoid serious Article III/Exceptions Clause difficulties while leaving some avenue for the Court to ensure uniformity. Accordingly, I would hold §2244(b)(1) inapplicable to §2255 motions and permit review here notwithstanding §2244(b)(3)(E).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA’s text and structure strongly indicate Congress meant the second-or-successive regime to prevent relitigation and promote finality, and it is most workable to apply §2244(b)(1)’s claim-repetition bar in the §2255 context alongside §2255(h)’s authorization categories. That reading fits AEDPA’s overall design and this Court’s recognition that AEDPA often yields strict, even “harsh,” results for diligent prisoners (Dodd v. United States), and it avoids a regime where identical claims can be re-presented repeatedly through renewed authorization applications. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly removes this Court’s certiorari review of courts of appeals’ gatekeeping decisions, and Felker v. Turpin upheld that withdrawal as a valid Exceptions Clause regulation in light of remaining avenues (including original habeas), so I would not create atextual carveouts to preserve review. Consistent with judicial restraint and institutional concerns, the Court should enforce the statute as written and leave any recalibration of successive-review mechanisms to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to “a habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not incorporate that subsection; instead, §2255(h) supplies two exclusive authorization categories, so importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar would add atextual limits and create superfluity with Congress’s chosen §2255(h) scheme. On reviewability, §2244(b)(3)(E) is best read narrowly to bar certiorari from the court of appeals’ grant/denial of authorization, but not to foreclose this Court from resolving the antecedent statutory question when the lower court’s disposition is not a qualifying “grant or denial,” consistent with the Court’s cautious approach to jurisdiction-stripping and the refusal to find implied repeals in habeas. Felker v. Turpin supports reading §2244(b)(3)(E) not to eliminate all avenues for this Court to perform its essential role, especially where an overbroad construction would raise serious Article III/Exceptions Clause concerns. AEDPA’s finality interests, emphasized in Dodd, cannot justify extending a restriction Congress wrote for §2254 into §2255 absent clear text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) sets out the exclusive gatekeeping criteria for federal prisoners; importing §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar into §2255 would add atextual restrictions and create unnecessary superfluity with §2255(h)(1)–(2), undermining procedural fairness in access to postconviction review. On the jurisdiction question, §2244(b)(3)(E) bars review of the “grant or denial” of authorization, but where the court of appeals “dismissed” on an asserted lack of jurisdiction while applying an arguably inapplicable gatekeeping rule, that disposition is best understood as a threshold legal determination outside (or at least not clearly within) (E)’s certiorari bar; absent a clear statement, we should not read (E) to foreclose this Court’s ability to resolve an important circuit conflict. Felker v. Turpin supports construing AEDPA’s jurisdiction-stripping provisions narrowly to avoid serious Article III/Exceptions Clause concerns and to preserve a meaningful role for this Court in maintaining uniformity of federal law. Practical consequences also matter: making later-presented claims categorically unreviewable based on earlier, often summary authorization papers would entrench error and inequity without clear congressional command, especially in the criminal-justice context.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s gatekeeping rule in 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1)—barring claims “presented in a prior application”—applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive collateral attacks brought under 28 U.S.C. §2255, and whether §2244(b)(3)(E) prevents Supreme Court certiorari review of courts of appeals’ authorization decisions in those §2255 cases.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1) and §2244(b)(3)(E) (AEDPA successive-petition provisions), as incorporated (or not) into 28 U.S.C. §2255 via §2255(h); related timing provision discussed: 28 U.S.C. §2255(f)(3).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1) by its text applies to state-prisoner habeas “applications” under §2254, not to federal-prisoner motions under §2255, and that importing §2244(b)(1) into §2255 is inconsistent with §2255(h)’s carefully limited cross-reference to §2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure (not §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim bar). He further contends that even if §2244(b)(3)(E) limits review of certain authorization rulings, it should not be read to strip the Supreme Court of certiorari jurisdiction in a way that blocks the Court’s core role in resolving entrenched circuit splits—especially given the reduced availability of alternative review mechanisms after Jones v. Hendrix and the resulting uniformity/Exceptions Clause concerns.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States maintains that §2244(b)(1) does apply to §2255 second-or-successive motions (as the Eleventh Circuit held), emphasizing AEDPA’s finality-oriented structure and arguing that Congress intended similar successive-application limits for state and federal prisoners. It also argues that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s command that authorization decisions ‘shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari’ forecloses Supreme Court certiorari review of authorization denials (and that contrary readings create administrability and asymmetry problems). Respondent additionally downplays fairness concerns, pointing to AEDPA’s intentionally harsh results (e.g., Dodd’s one-year limit running from initial recognition of a right even before retroactivity is decided), and argues federal prisoners typically have multiple earlier opportunities to raise claims (trial/direct appeal/first §2255) before §2244(b)(1) is implicated.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (statement respecting denial of certiorari by Justice Kavanaugh)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (statement respecting denial by Justice Sotomayor joined by Justice Jackson)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s integrated-scheme/loophole argument is the strongest pushback: “certified as provided in section 2244” could be read to pull in §2244(b)(1)’s repeat-claim bar to serve AEDPA’s finality aims. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, the only part of §2244 that actually describes the certification mechanism is §2244(b)(3); importing §2244(b)(1)’s separate, §2254-“application” rule by implication would awkwardly overlay and potentially displace Congress’s specifically calibrated §2255(h)(1)–(2) limits for federal prisoners. On jurisdiction, Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s text is categorical and Felker upheld it, yet Felker’s avoidance-inflected approach and the absence of an unmistakable clear statement to extend (E) through §2255(h)’s cross-reference counsel a narrow construction here—especially given Jones v. Hendrix’s contraction of alternative review paths. Under minimalist, precedent-respecting principles, I would decide only what is necessary: §2255(h) incorporates §2244(b)(3)’s procedure (and not §2244(b)(1) or a broader certiorari bar) absent clearer congressional direction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s argument (joined by Justice Kagan) that §2255(h) borrows only §2244(b)(3)’s mechanics because it alone describes “how to certify” reads the cross-reference too narrowly; Congress said “certified as provided in section 2244,” not “as provided in subsection (b)(3),” and the ordinary meaning of that phrase incorporates the gatekeeping framework Congress enacted in §2244(b), including the basic bar on re-presented claims in (b)(1). Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Felker-based clear-statement/avoidance concerns do not permit us to soften §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical command that authorization decisions “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari,” especially because Felker upheld Congress’s withdrawal of certiorari as a permissible jurisdictional regulation. Post–Jones v. Hendrix consequences and entrenched splits are policy concerns, but under a strict textualist/originalist approach we enforce AEDPA’s jurisdictional and gatekeeping limits as written. No colleague has supplied a textual basis to treat the §2255 cross-reference as selectively importing only the procedural subset while ignoring the integrated successive-application restrictions that give the certification requirement its content.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I am not persuaded by the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s textual point that §2255(h)’s phrase “certified as provided in section 2244” necessarily imports only §2244(b)(3)’s mechanics: that reading treats the cross-reference as an atextual pick-and-choose and undermines AEDPA’s integrated successive-litigation regime by allowing repetitive re-packaging of the same claim through serial authorization requests. Justice Thomas’s integrated-scheme argument better fits how Congress wrote the cross-reference—“section 2244,” not “subsection (b)(3)”—and it is entirely natural that §2255(h)(1)–(2) adds prisoner-specific thresholds on top of, rather than in lieu of, §2244’s baseline anti-duplication premise. On jurisdiction, Justice Sotomayor’s post–Jones v. Hendrix concern about entrenched splits is consequential, but it cannot justify narrowing §2244(b)(3)(E)’s unqualified “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari,” and Felker’s approval of that withdrawal confirms we must enforce the clear limitation even if the policy consequences are harsh. Nothing in colleagues’ avoidance arguments supplies a clear-statement basis to rewrite either the incorporated gatekeeping structure or the jurisdictional bar.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the “integrated scheme/loophole” concern: that reading §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” to import only §2244(b)(3) lets repeat claims cycle through authorization requests. But that structural intuition cannot supply text Congress did not write, particularly where §2255(h)(1)–(2) already provide the substantive successive-motion limits for federal prisoners and §2244(b)(3) is the only portion that actually prescribes how “certification” occurs. On the certiorari bar, Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh correctly emphasize §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical language and Felker, yet Felker’s acceptance was intertwined with preserving other Supreme Court review avenues; after Jones v. Hendrix narrowed alternative routes, extending (E) to §2255 via an indirect cross-reference would entrench liberty-affecting circuit splits absent a clear statement. Under my pragmatic, text-faithful approach attentive to real-world consequences for incarcerated people, I would not amplify AEDPA’s harshness by implication when Congress chose narrower words.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett press the strongest point: that “certified as provided in section 2244” naturally incorporates all of §2244(b), including (b)(1), to avoid the “loophole” Justice Alito worries about. But on a pragmatic textualist read, “certified as provided” most directly points to the provisions that actually prescribe the certification mechanism—§2244(b)(3)—while importing §2244(b)(1)’s separate relitigation bar would awkwardly superadd a categorical limit atop §2255(h)(1)–(2)’s tailored federal-prisoner gateways and risk displacing that calibrated design by implication. On jurisdiction, Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker is substantial, yet Felker’s narrow, non-expansive approach to habeas jurisdiction counsels against extending (E) to §2255 authorization orders via an indirect cross-reference absent a clearer statement, especially given the post–Jones v. Hendrix landscape. I therefore remain with petitioner because respondent’s integrated-scheme arguments do not overcome the more coherent textual fit between §2255(h) and §2244(b)(3) specifically.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett’s integrated-scheme/loophole point is the respondent’s strongest: “certified as provided in section 2244” could be read to sweep in §2244(b)(1)’s repeat-claim bar. But on a textualist reading, the only thing §2244 “provides” about how a claim gets “certified” is §2244(b)(3)’s gatekeeping procedure; importing §2244(b)(1)’s separate substantive rule—written for a state-prisoner “application” under §2254—adds a categorical limitation Congress conspicuously did not place in §2255(h)(1)–(2). On jurisdiction, Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker is weighty, yet Felker’s own caution against expansive habeas jurisdiction-stripping and its reliance on other review avenues counsel against extending (E) to §2255 via an indirect cross-reference absent a clear statement—especially post–Jones v. Hendrix, where alternative corrective paths have narrowed. Structural worries about repetitive filings cannot override enacted text, so I remain with petitioner on both questions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point—that §2255(h)’s cross-reference most naturally imports only §2244(b)(3)’s certification mechanics—is the most serious challenge to my view, and I take it as a close call. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett stress, reading “certified as provided in section 2244” to exclude §2244(b)(1)’s re-presented-claim bar fractures AEDPA’s integrated successive-petition design and leaves the gatekeeping regime oddly incomplete for federal prisoners, inviting repetitive filings that Congress plainly meant to curtail. On the certiorari question, Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Felker and post–Jones v. Hendrix practical consequences does not overcome §2244(b)(3)(E)’s unqualified “shall not” language; Felker upheld that jurisdictional withdrawal, and institutional concerns cannot justify narrowing clear text. No argument raised in this round supplies a principled textual basis to carve §2255 authorizations out of (E) or to selectively incorporate only parts of §2244 while claiming fidelity to what Congress enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is textual: as he notes, §2255(h) speaks of being “certified as provided in section 2244,” and the subsection that actually prescribes certification mechanics is §2244(b)(3). But Justice Thomas’s integrated-scheme reading better fits the enacted cross-reference as written—Congress did not say “as provided in subsection (b)(3),” and the §2244 gatekeeping framework presupposes that previously presented claims are not eligible for authorization at all, making (b)(1) part of what “as provided in section 2244” naturally imports. On certiorari, Justice Sotomayor’s Felker/Jones avoidance concern is serious, yet §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical withdrawal of certiorari is the sort of clear jurisdictional command we usually enforce, and Felker supports that result so long as the Court’s jurisdiction is not eliminated wholesale. Because those counterarguments do not identify ambiguity sufficient to justify a narrowing construction under my textualist methodology, I remain with respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s integrated-scheme/“loophole” argument is the strongest push, but it still asks us—without clear textual direction—to graft §2244(b)(1)’s §2254-specific relitigation bar onto §2255(h), even though Congress separately and precisely set §2255(h)(1)–(2)’s substantive gates for federal prisoners. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, the only part of §2244 that actually tells courts how to "certif[y]" is §2244(b)(3), so reading “certified as provided in section 2244” to import the certification process rather than every substantive limit is the more coherent, administrable construction. On certiorari, Justice Kavanaugh is right that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s language is blunt and Felker upheld it, but Felker’s acceptance depended on preserved avenues of Supreme Court review; after Jones v. Hendrix, extending (E) via an indirect §2255 cross-reference would have severe practical consequences for liberty and uniformity without the kind of clear statement I would require for jurisdiction stripping. Under my pragmatic, text-centered approach, respondent’s structural concerns cannot justify enlarging AEDPA’s bars or insulating authorization decisions from review beyond what Congress unmistakably enacted.

John Roberts.reasoning: On the first question, §2244(b)(1) by its terms regulates claims "presented in a prior application" in the §2254 state-prisoner habeas framework, and §2255(h) cross-references only §2244(b)(3)’s certification procedure rather than importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim bar; reading (b)(1) into §2255 risks overriding Congress’s more tailored successive-motion limits in §2255(h)(1)–(2). On the second question, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s "no certiorari" language should be read narrowly in light of the clear-statement principle for jurisdiction-stripping and this Court’s admonition that "repeals by implication are not favored" in habeas, see Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651, 660 (1996). A narrow construction that preserves this Court’s ability to resolve entrenched circuit splits also avoids serious Exceptions Clause concerns flagged in Felker, while still respecting AEDPA’s finality interests through §2255(h)’s stringent gatekeeping. Accordingly, I would reverse on both questions on the narrowest textual grounds available.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 2255(h) expressly requires a federal prisoner seeking to file a second-or-successive motion to proceed through “the appropriate court of appeals as provided in section 2244,” and that cross-reference is best read (consistent with AEDPA’s text and finality-focused structure) to incorporate AEDPA’s successive-claim limits, including §2244(b)(1)’s bar on claims “presented in a prior application,” rather than to create a looser federal-prisoner regime by omission. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s plain text—authorization determinations “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of … a writ of certiorari”—forecloses this Court’s certiorari review of courts of appeals’ gatekeeping decisions in the §2255 context once Congress has made that “exception[] and regulation[]” to appellate jurisdiction. Felker v. Turpin confirms that Congress may withdraw certiorari review of gatekeeping determinations without violating Article III, particularly where (as there) other avenues are not categorically eliminated, and Jones v. Hendrix underscores that courts must apply AEDPA’s restrictions as written even when the result is harsh. Whatever policy concerns exist, they cannot justify rewriting §§2244 and 2255 to expand collateral review beyond the statute’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA’s successive-petition regime is structured to promote finality and to prevent repetitive relitigation, and reading §2255(h)’s cross-reference to §2244(b)(3) to leave federal prisoners free of §2244(b)(1)’s bar on claims “presented in a prior application” would create a loophole inconsistent with that design and with the practical consequences Congress plainly sought. The better textual reading is that, once a §2255 movant invokes the (b)(3) gatekeeping mechanism for a “second or successive” filing, the associated AEDPA limitations on re-presented claims apply in that setting as well, otherwise the certification procedure would do little work against duplicative claims. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides that the authorization decision “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari,” and unlike in Felker (which preserved original habeas and counseled against implied repeals), this is a clear statement foreclosing certiorari review of authorization rulings; any fairness concerns are for Congress, and this Court has enforced AEDPA’s harsh timing and finality choices as written, see Dodd v. United States. Practical administrability also favors the Government’s view, avoiding asymmetric review of “dismissals” versus “denials” and preserving a bright-line rule at the gatekeeping stage.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms bars claims “presented in a prior application,” and that language is directed at state-prisoner habeas “applications” under §2254; Congress chose in §2255(h) to cross-reference only §2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure, not §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim bar, and we should not expand AEDPA’s restrictions beyond the text where doing so would foreclose meaningful review for federal prisoners. Reading §2244(b)(3)(E) to strip this Court of certiorari review over §2255 authorization decisions would exacerbate entrenched circuit splits and, after Jones v. Hendrix, risks leaving federal prisoners with no viable path for this Court to perform its essential uniformity function, triggering the constitutional concerns Justice Souter flagged in Felker v. Turpin. Felker upheld the certiorari bar only because other avenues of Supreme Court review—most notably original habeas—remained available; that premise is substantially undermined in the post–Jones landscape, especially for prisoners asserting new statutory-innocence or similarly fundamental claims. Given AEDPA’s harsh timing and retroactivity traps (see Dodd v. United States), a narrow, text-faithful reading that preserves access to corrective process is both legally sound and necessary to avoid unjust and irreparable consequences for vulnerable litigants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms bars claims “presented in a prior application,” and in AEDPA that language is drafted for state-prisoner “applications” under §2254; Congress did not incorporate that categorical claim-bar into §2255, instead making a targeted cross-reference in §2255(h) to §2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure. Reading §2244(b)(1) into §2255 would override the specific, carefully delimited gateways in §2255(h)(1)–(2) and create statutory incoherence (including friction with §2255(f)(3)’s timing rule), so the better textual and workable reading is that §2244(b)(1) does not apply in §2255 cases. As to §2244(b)(3)(E), Felker v. Turpin shows the Court should construe AEDPA’s review-limiting provisions narrowly where possible to avoid serious Article III/Exceptions Clause concerns and to preserve the Court’s essential role in maintaining uniformity; at minimum, (E) should not be read to foreclose certiorari over courts of appeals’ §2255 authorization dispositions in a way that leaves entrenched circuit splits unresolvable. That narrower reading respects Congress’s gatekeeping design while avoiding unnecessary constitutional doubts and administrability problems.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs a “claim presented in a prior application” under the §2254 framework, and Congress in §2255(h) cross-referenced only “the appropriate court of appeals” certification procedure in §2244(b)(3), not §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim bar—so importing (b)(1) into §2255 would disregard the enacted text and upset §2255(h)’s calibrated limits. As for review, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on certiorari is clearest as applied in the §2254 context addressed in Felker; extending it to foreclose this Court’s certiorari review of §2255 authorization decisions would require an unmistakably clear statement, especially where it would effectively insulate entrenched circuit splits from this Court’s ordinary supervisory role. Felker upheld (E) in part because other avenues of Supreme Court review (including original habeas) remained available, while noting that if those avenues closed the Exceptions Clause question would be open—concerns sharpened after Jones v. Hendrix narrowed alternative collateral pathways. Reading §2255(h) and §2244(b)(3)(E) according to their plain terms therefore favors petitioner on both the successive-claim rule and this Court’s certiorari jurisdiction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA’s successive-petition regime is a finality-focused, workability-driven framework, and §2255(h)’s incorporation of §2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure is best read in context to carry with it the core gatekeeping consequence that previously presented claims may not be relitigated in a second-or-successive collateral attack, consistent with AEDPA’s structure and Congress’s evident effort to align state and federal postconviction limits. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s text—authorization decisions “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of … a writ of certiorari”—is a clear jurisdiction-stripping command, and under Felker v. Turpin we should enforce that limitation while avoiding any unnecessary constitutional holding because some avenue of Supreme Court supervisory review can remain via original habeas in appropriate circumstances. Practical administrability also favors the government’s reading: permitting certiorari review of some authorization outcomes (e.g., “dismissals”) but not others would produce asymmetry and uncertainty in a process Congress designed to be swift and final. This result is consistent with our prior approach to AEDPA’s harsh but textually compelled rules, see Dodd v. United States, and with judicial restraint in the face of Congress’s chosen gatekeeping design.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, §2255(h) requires that a second-or-successive federal-prisoner motion “must be certified as provided in section 2244,” and the better reading of that cross-reference—given AEDPA’s integrated successive-petition scheme—is that Congress meant §2244’s gatekeeping framework to apply to §2255 second-or-successive litigation, including the claim-preclusion rule in §2244(b)(1). Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides that an authorization decision “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of…a writ of certiorari,” and under Felker v. Turpin that jurisdiction-stripping is constitutionally permissible so long as some avenues of Supreme Court review (e.g., original habeas in appropriate circumstances) remain. While petitioner’s structural arguments have force, methodological consistency and AEDPA’s finality-oriented design (reflected in decisions like Dodd v. United States and Jones v. Hendrix) counsel adhering to the statute’s plain prohibition on certiorari review of authorization rulings and applying the same successive-claim constraints to §2255 motions. Any residual constitutional concern does not justify rewriting §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical text, and Congress’s choice to tighten collateral review must be respected.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to habeas “applications” under §2254 and is not among the provisions Congress cross-referenced in §2255(h), which incorporates only the §2244(b)(3) authorization procedure; reading (b)(1) into §2255 would override §2255(h)’s carefully drawn limits and create avoidable unfairness for federal prisoners seeking to raise newly available constitutional claims. As to §2244(b)(3)(E), Felker v. Turpin counsels against construing AEDPA to foreclose this Court’s ability to ensure uniformity of federal law absent a clear statement and an alternative avenue of review, and the post–Jones v. Hendrix landscape heightens the practical consequences of a jurisdiction-stripping reading. A narrower construction—treating (E) as barring party-initiated review only of true “grant/deny” authorization determinations, while leaving room for certiorari where the court of appeals never made the requisite §2244(b)(3) determination—best fits the text and avoids serious Exceptions Clause concerns. That approach also promotes procedural fairness and preserves this Court’s role in resolving entrenched circuit splits affecting liberty.
